opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core motivation comes from looking at how humans and animals learn. A huge amount of what we know about the world, especially early on, isn't learned from labels or explicit supervision, and it's not even learned primarily through interaction. Infants spend their first months mostly just watching. They pick up object permanence, intuitive physics like gravity and solidity, and how things tend to move, largely by observing the world unfold in front of them. That suggests there's an enormous amount of structure you can extract just from passive sensory input.

From a machine learning perspective, that's really appealing because observational data is abundant. There's essentially an unlimited supply of images and video, and if we can learn good representations from that without human annotation, we're no longer bottlenecked by labeling. Labels are also a fairly impoverished signal. A class label compresses a rich scene into a single token, whereas the raw data contains far more information about the world.

The key question then is what objective you use to learn from that data. A lot of earlier approaches either relied on hand-crafted data augmentations, as in invariance-based methods, which bake in strong human priors about what should or shouldn't matter, or they reconstructed pixels, which forces the model to spend capacity on low-level details that are often unpredictable and not very semantically useful. The direction we've been pushing, with joint-embedding predictive architectures like I-JEPA and V-JEPA, is to predict missing or future parts of the input in an abstract representation space rather than in pixel space. The model sees part of an image or video and has to predict the representations of the parts it doesn't see. That lets it focus on the predictable, high-level structure, like what objects are there and how they're moving, and ignore the noise.

Video in particular is exciting because time gives you a natural prediction signal. Predicting how a scene evolves pushes the model toward understanding motion, dynamics, and eventually something like a world model. And we've seen that these representations transfer well, often with a frozen backbone, to downstream tasks, sometimes even ones that require fine-grained motion understanding. So passive observation isn't the whole story. Eventually you want agents that act and plan. But it's a very strong foundation to build that on, and arguably the most scalable one we have.

r001.rationale: The response says observational data is abundant, with an essentially unlimited supply of images and video, making learning without human annotation possible.

r002.rationale: It compares AI learning from passive sensory input with infants and animals acquiring understanding of the world by watching rather than relying on labels or interaction.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it starts with a simple observation about how humans and animals actually acquire most of what they know. If you look at an infant in its first few months of life, it isn't being given labels, and it isn't really acting in the world in any sophisticated way either. It can barely control its limbs. And yet in that window it's forming an enormous amount of structured knowledge about the world: that objects are solid, that they persist when they go out of view, that unsupported things fall, that things move along smooth trajectories. All of that comes largely from just watching. The sensory stream is incredibly rich, and the brain is extracting regularities from it without anyone telling it what to look for.

So from a machine learning perspective, that's a really compelling signal. Labels are expensive and they're always going to be a tiny fraction of the available data. Interaction, in the reinforcement learning sense, is expensive too, and often slow or unsafe. But passive observation, raw images and video, is essentially unlimited. If you can build learning objectives that let a model pull out that same kind of structure, the physics, the object-level regularities, the way scenes evolve over time, then you're tapping into a source of supervision that scales with the amount of data you can collect rather than with how much human annotation you can afford.

The other thing I'd say is that video in particular is interesting because it has a built-in notion of prediction. The world at time t plus one is highly constrained by the world at time t, and so you can ask a model to predict what's going to happen, or to predict what's hidden in part of a scene, and the only way to do that well is to understand the content. That's very different from classification, where you can often get away with shortcuts. And a lot of what we've been working on, with the joint-embedding predictive approaches, is trying to make that prediction happen in a learned representation space rather than at the pixel level. Pixel-level prediction forces the model to waste capacity on things that are fundamentally unpredictable, the exact texture of leaves rustling in the wind, for example, whereas in representation space the model can learn to ignore that noise and focus on the semantically meaningful, predictable structure.

So to me the promise is really that: you have an essentially unlimited data source, you have a natural learning signal in the form of prediction, and you have biological evidence that this kind of learning actually works and gets you a long way toward a model of the world. I think of it as the foundation that other capabilities, like planning and acting, can then be built on top of.

r001.rationale: It says passive observation of raw images and video is “essentially unlimited,” unlike scarce labels and costly interaction.

r002.rationale: It compares machine learning from observation with infants and animals gaining structured knowledge about the world largely by watching.

astra-6.text:
I think what’s exciting about passive observation is how much structure there is in the world that we don’t need someone to label for us. If you watch an object move through a scene, you get information about that object, how it relates to other objects, and how the world evolves over time. That’s a very rich learning signal, even if you’re not taking any actions yourself.

The challenge is figuring out what to predict. With images and video, there are lots of details that are difficult to predict and may not be relevant to understanding the scene. If you’re watching a tree blowing in the wind, you probably don’t need to predict the exact position of every leaf. You want a representation that captures the underlying structure and allows you to reason about what could happen next.

So the promise of self-supervised learning is that we can learn those representations from the observations themselves, without requiring a human to annotate every example. Passive observation may not give us everything we need for intelligence, but it seems like a powerful way to build a foundation that we can then use for more specific tasks or for learning through interaction.

r001.rationale: The response describes passive observations as a rich learning signal, but does not identify access to vast quantities of data as an advantage.

r002.rationale: The response discusses learning from observations without labels, but does not compare AI learning to how humans acquire understanding through passive observation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the most compelling things about passive observation is just how much structure there is in the world that we don’t need someone to label for us. If you watch an object move through a scene, you get information about its shape, how it interacts with other objects, and what tends to happen next. Video gives you this very rich learning signal essentially for free.

The challenge is figuring out the right prediction task. If you try to predict every pixel in a future frame, you spend a lot of effort modeling details that may be unpredictable or aren’t relevant to understanding the scene. You don’t necessarily need to know exactly how every leaf will move to understand that there’s a tree blowing in the wind. So an appealing direction is to learn representations in which you can predict the more meaningful aspects of what you observe.

And the scalability is really exciting. There’s an enormous amount of image and video data available without annotations. If we can learn useful representations from that, then we can build systems that require much less labeled data when we want to adapt them to a particular task. Passive observation probably isn’t the whole story—interaction matters too—but it seems like a powerful foundation.

r001.rationale: The response says there is an “enormous amount” of unannotated image and video data available, identifying the scale of available data as an advantage.

r002.rationale: The response discusses passive observation as a learning source for AI, but does not compare it to how humans acquire understanding through passive observation.
